quests.instruction: On a voicemail you hear “Hi Mia, did you get my message?” Which spoken form of “did you get” is typical?
quests.word: Hi Mia, did you get my message
quests.textToSpeak: Hi Mia, did you get my message
options: “di-ja get”: a /dʒ/ blend replaces the /d/ and the /j/
“did you get”: three strong words with a clear /j/
“di-ya get”: the /d/ is dropped before the weak “you”
“di-cha get”: the blend is /tʃ/ because “get” follows
quests.correctAnswer: “di-ja get”: a /dʒ/ blend replaces the /d/ and the /j/
quests.hint: Say the first half of the sentence at voicemail speed, and listen to what happens between “did” and “you”.
quests.explanation: On the phone people speak quickly, and “did you” is one of the first things to fuse: the /d/ and the /j/ become /dʒ/, and “you” is weak. So you hear “di-ja get”. The /t/ of “get” is a separate sound and plays no part in the blend. Knowing this helps you understand voicemails that sound like “dija”.
quests.phoneticRule: Fast, phone-style delivery encourages blending of /d/ + /j/, and the following word does not affect the result.
quests.spokenForm: Hi Mia, di-ja get my message

quests.instruction: Why does “text you” sound like “teks-chu” in “Jack will text you later”?
options: The /s/ and the /j/ blend into /ʃ/, and the /t/ is lost from the cluster
The /k/ and /s/ blend together into a new sound with the /j/ following
The /t/ is lost and the /j/ is kept clear: “teks-you”
The final /t/ meets the /j/ of “you” and they blend into /tʃ/ after the /s/
quests.correctAnswer: The final /t/ meets the /j/ of “you” and they blend into /tʃ/ after the /s/
quests.hint: Find the last sound of “text” and the first sound of “you”. Which of the four blends could they form?
quests.explanation: “Text” ends in /kst/, and the last sound is /t/. That /t/ meets /j/, so the pair blends into /tʃ/: “teks-chu”. The /s/ before it stays as it is. Words that end in a cluster follow the same rule as single consonants: only the last sound enters the blend.
quests.phoneticRule: In a final consonant cluster, only the last sound blends with a following /j/; the earlier consonants stay.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “missed your” fits “Sorry, I missed your call”?
options: “miss-tyour”: both sounds are kept apart, with a clear /j/
“mis-chyer”: the /t/ and a weak “your” blend into /tʃ/
“mis-jyer”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/
“mis-yer”: the /t/ is dropped and the /j/ is kept
quests.correctAnswer: “mis-chyer”: the /t/ and a weak “your” blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: The past-tense ending of “missed” is a /t/. Predict its blend with the /j/ of “your”.
quests.explanation: The ending of “missed” is /t/, and “your” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /tʃ/: “mis-chyer”. This is a good reminder that past-tense endings take part in the blends. On a call, hearing “mis-chyer” should bring “missed your” to mind.
quests.phoneticRule: Past-tense /t/ and /d/ endings blend with a following /j/ just as lexical /t/ and /d/ do.

quests.instruction: At a theatre you hear “Find your seat, please.” Which spoken form of “find your” fits?
options: “find-your”: both words are strong with a clear /j/
“fine-chyer”: the blend is /tʃ/ after the /n/
“fine-jyer”: the /d/ and a weak “your” blend into /dʒ/
“fine-yer”: the /d/ is dropped and the /j/ is kept
quests.correctAnswer: “fine-jyer”: the /d/ and a weak “your” blend into /dʒ/
quests.hint: Say the instruction as an usher would, quickly and kindly. Listen to the sound between “find” and “your”.
quests.explanation: “Find” ends in the cluster /nd/, and the last sound, /d/, meets the /j/ of “your”. They blend into /dʒ/: “fine-jyer”. The /n/ stays. Instructions like this one use the blend almost every time they are spoken at normal speed.
quests.phoneticRule: Instructions with an imperative verb ending in /d/ followed by “your” are a common place for /d/ + /j/ to blend.

quests.instruction: In “Raise your hand if you agree”, which sound does the /z/ of “raise” become before “your”?
quests.word: Raise your hand if you agree
quests.textToSpeak: Raise your hand if you agree
options: /dʒ/, as in “jam”: “ray-jyer” instead
/ʃ/, as in “shoe”: “ray-shyer” instead
/ʒ/, as in “vision”: “ray-zhyer”
/z/ is unchanged and a clear /j/ follows
quests.correctAnswer: /ʒ/, as in “vision”: “ray-zhyer”
quests.hint: The /z/ is voiced. Pick a blend that keeps that buzz and is a smooth fricative.
quests.explanation: “Raise” ends in /z/ and “your” begins with /j/, so the result is /ʒ/: “ray-zhyer”. The second “you” in the sentence, in “if you”, does not blend because “if” ends in /f/, which is not one of the four triggers. So the sentence contains exactly one blend.
quests.phoneticRule: Only /t/, /d/, /s/ and /z/ blend with /j/; other consonants, such as /f/, leave the /j/ unchanged.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “lost your” in “Lost your keys again?” Which spoken form fits?
options: “los-chyer”: the /t/ and a weak “your” blend into /tʃ/
“lost-your”: both words are strong and separate
“los-shyer”: the /t/ is lost and the /s/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/
“los-jyer”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: “los-chyer”: the /t/ and a weak “your” blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: Isolate the final /t/ of “lost” and recall what a /t/ becomes before /j/.
quests.explanation: “Lost” ends in /st/, and the last sound, /t/, blends with /j/ into /tʃ/: “los-chyer”. A sympathetic question like this is usually said quickly, so the blend is very likely. If you only listened for a clear “lost your”, you could miss it.
quests.phoneticRule: The same last-sound rule applies to /st/ clusters: the /t/ blends, and the /s/ is retained.

quests.instruction: Which processes are heard in “So what do you want?”
options: A strong “do” and a clear separate /j/ before “you”
A weak “do” whose /d/ blends with “you” into /dʒ/, plus weak “you”
Elision of the /d/ and a /j/ glide linking “do” to “you”
Assimilation of the /d/ to the /w/ of “what”, and a strong, fully pronounced “you”
quests.correctAnswer: A weak “do” whose /d/ blends with “you” into /dʒ/, plus weak “you”
quests.hint: Listen to the three small words in the middle of the question and decide how many of them are strong.
quests.explanation: “What do you want” is stressed on “what” and “want”. The three words between them are weak, and the /d/ of “do” blends with the /j/ of “you” into /dʒ/. You hear something like “wot-dja want”. This is the classic fast form of the question, built from a weak “do”, a blend and a weak “you”.
quests.phoneticRule: A weak auxiliary “do” followed by weak “you” forms a single quick unit in which /d/ + /j/ gives /dʒ/.

quests.instruction: Which two blends are heard in “Carl, did you lose your keys?”
quests.word: Carl, did you lose your keys
quests.textToSpeak: Carl, did you lose your keys
options: /tʃ/ in “did you” and /ʒ/ in “lose your”
/dʒ/ in “did you” and /ʃ/ in “lose your”
/ʒ/ in “did you” and /dʒ/ in “lose your”
/dʒ/ in “did you” and /ʒ/ in “lose your”
quests.correctAnswer: /dʒ/ in “did you” and /ʒ/ in “lose your”
quests.hint: Work out each junction separately: the last sound of the first word decides the blend.
quests.explanation: “Did” ends in voiced /d/ and “lose” ends in voiced /z/. A voiced stop blends to /dʒ/, and a voiced fricative blends to /ʒ/. So you hear “di-ja loo-zhyer”. Two different blends can therefore appear in the same question, and each is chosen by its own first sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Each junction in a sentence is evaluated separately, so a stop-plus-/j/ and a fricative-plus-/j/ give different results.

quests.instruction: Why does “can you” in “Omar, can you help me?” not blend into a “ch” or “j” sound like “did you” does?
options: “can” is stressed, which blocks every blend
The /n/ is voiced, and voiced sounds do not blend with /j/
The /n/ is a nasal, not a stop or fricative, so the /j/ stays separate
“you” is too weak to cause a blend after “can”
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ is a nasal, not a stop or fricative, so the /j/ stays separate
quests.hint: Recall the four sounds that blend with /j/ and check whether /n/ is one of them.
quests.explanation: Only /t/, /d/, /s/ and /z/ blend with /j/ in this way. /n/ is a nasal, so “can you” is said with a clear /j/, often as “kin-yoo”. That means you can tell “did you” (blend) from “can you” (no blend) by listening for the “j” sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence is limited to the alveolar stops and fricatives /t d s z/; nasals and liquids keep a separate /j/.

quests.instruction: Compare “did he” in “Hugo, did he call?” with “did you”. What happens at “did he”?
options: The /h/ is dropped and the /d/ links onto the vowel: “di-dee”, no blend
The /d/ and the /h/ blend together into a /dʒ/ sound
The /d/ is dropped completely before the weak “he”, leaving only “di” and a vowel behind
The /d/ and the vowel of “he” blend together into /dʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: The /h/ is dropped and the /d/ links onto the vowel: “di-dee”, no blend
quests.hint: A blend needs a /j/. Check what sound begins “he” once the /h/ is dropped.
quests.explanation: When the /h/ of “he” is dropped, the word begins with a vowel, not a /j/. So there is nothing to blend with, and the /d/ simply links onto the vowel: “di-dee”. The blend /dʒ/ belongs to “did you”, not to “did he”. Telling the two apart is a useful listening skill.
quests.phoneticRule: Dropping /h/ produces a vowel-initial word that triggers linking, not coalescence, because coalescence requires a following /j/.

quests.instruction: In “Priya, did you miss her call?”, which junction blends and which only links?
quests.word: Priya, did you miss her call
quests.textToSpeak: Priya, did you miss her call
options: Both blend: /dʒ/ in “did you” and /ʃ/ in “miss her”
“did you” blends into /dʒ/, while “miss her” only links the /s/ onto “her”
“miss her” blends into /ʃ/ and “did you” only links the /d/ onto the next word
Neither: both junctions keep their separate sounds
quests.correctAnswer: “did you” blends into /dʒ/, while “miss her” only links the /s/ onto “her”
quests.hint: Check the first sound of each second word: is it /j/ or a vowel?
quests.explanation: “You” begins with /j/, so “did you” blends. “Her”, with its /h/ dropped, begins with a vowel, so “miss her” only links the /s/ onto it: “mi-ser”. The same sentence thus contains one blend and one link. Both are normal.
quests.phoneticRule: The first sound of the second word decides the process: /j/ gives coalescence, and a vowel gives linking.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “let her” fits “Carl will let her go”?
options: “le-chər”: the /t/ and /h/ blend into /tʃ/
“let-her”: both sounds fully pronounced, with a pause between the two words
“le-ər”: the /t/ and /h/ are both dropped
“le-tər”: the /h/ is dropped and the /t/ links onto “her”, with no blend
quests.correctAnswer: “le-tər”: the /h/ is dropped and the /t/ links onto “her”, with no blend
quests.hint: Compare “let her” with “let you”, and decide which of them has a /j/ to trigger a blend.
quests.explanation: “Her” loses its /h/ and begins with a vowel, so the /t/ of “let” links onto it: “le-tər”. A blend into /tʃ/ would require a /j/, as in “let you”. So “let her” and “let you” sound different, and the difference tells you which pronoun was said.
quests.phoneticRule: “Let her” (a link) and “let you” (a blend) differ by one sound; the /tʃ/ is a cue that the pronoun was “you”.

quests.instruction: In a formal interview you say, “Sir, would you repeat that?” Which delivery is acceptable?
options: Only “wou-ja” is acceptable, because blends are required in English
Only the clear “would you” is acceptable, because blends are considered impolite
Neither is acceptable in an interview; the phrase must be avoided
Both “wou-ja” and a clear “would you” are acceptable in careful speech
quests.correctAnswer: Both “wou-ja” and a clear “would you” are acceptable in careful speech
quests.hint: Ask whether connected speech is a rule or a tendency that depends on style.
quests.explanation: Blending is typical of fast, relaxed speech, but it is not compulsory. In a formal setting, a speaker may keep the /d/ and /j/ apart, and a listener will understand perfectly. For you as a listener, the key is to recognise both versions of the same phrase.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence is optional and style-dependent: careful speech may preserve the original sounds without sounding incorrect.

quests.instruction: Two speakers say “Could you pass me the salt?” One says “cou-ja”, the other says “could you” clearly. Which statement is accurate?
quests.word: Mia, could you pass me the salt
quests.textToSpeak: Mia, could you pass me the salt
options: The second speaker is more careful; the blend is normal fast speech, not an error
The first speaker is wrong, because the blend changes the meaning of the word
The second speaker is wrong, because English requires the blend in every phrase
Both speakers are wrong, because every sound should be kept fully separate in good speech
quests.correctAnswer: The second speaker is more careful; the blend is normal fast speech, not an error
quests.hint: Think of the blend as a speed-and-style choice rather than a correctness rule.
quests.explanation: Both versions are normal; they differ in style. The blend is a natural result of fast speech, and the clear version is a natural result of careful speech. Neither is an error. Treating the blend as a mistake would make everyday speech sound wrong, which is not the case.
quests.phoneticRule: Blended and unblended forms are variants of the same phrase; neither is a mistake, and the choice reflects speed and formality.
quests.spokenForm: Mia, cou-ja pass me the salt

quests.instruction: Someone says “Won’t YOU listen to me?” with strong stress on “you”. What happens to the blend?
options: The blend is more likely, because stressed words are louder and clearer
The /t/ is dropped completely, so “won’t” loses its final sound
The stressed “you” keeps a clear /j/ and the blend is less likely
The blend becomes /ʃ/ because the vowel of “you” is longer
quests.correctAnswer: The stressed “you” keeps a clear /j/ and the blend is less likely
quests.hint: Remember that blends are helped by weak /jə/. What changes when “you” is stressed?
quests.explanation: A stressed “you” has a full vowel, /juː/, and a clear /j/, so the junction with /t/ tends to stay separate: “wohnt YOU”. The blend is much more typical when “you” is weak. Listening for stress therefore tells you whether to expect a blend.
quests.phoneticRule: Stress on “you” restores its full form and reduces the likelihood of coalescence, which is favoured by the weak form /jə/.

quests.instruction: Someone sneezes and you say “Bless you.” Which spoken form fits?
options: “bless-you”: both sounds are separate
“bleh-shoo”: the /s/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/
“bleh-choo”: they blend into /tʃ/, like a sneeze
“bleh-zhoo”: they blend into /ʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: “bleh-shoo”: the /s/ and /j/ blend into /ʃ/
quests.hint: A sneeze is “achoo”, but this blend is a different one. Check the last sound of “bless”.
quests.explanation: “Bless” ends in /s/, so with /j/ the result is /ʃ/: “bleh-shoo”. The “ch” of a sneeze, “a-choo”, is /tʃ/, which would need a /t/. This is a small reminder that each blend is tied to its first sound.
quests.phoneticRule: The blend /ʃ/ in “bless you” follows from /s/ + /j/; /tʃ/ would require a /t/ before the /j/.

quests.instruction: Someone bumps into you and says “Excuse you!” What happens where “excuse” and “you” meet?
options: The /z/ and /j/ blend into the voiceless /ʃ/: “ex-cue-shoo”
The /z/ and /j/ blend into the stop /dʒ/: “ex-cue-joo”
The /z/ and /j/ blend into /ʒ/: “ex-cue-zhoo”
The two sounds stay separate and are both pronounced: “ex-cuse-you”
quests.correctAnswer: The /z/ and /j/ blend into /ʒ/: “ex-cue-zhoo”
quests.hint: “Excuse” in this phrase ends in a voiced /z/. Choose the blend that keeps the voicing.
quests.explanation: As a verb, “excuse” ends in /z/, so with /j/ it becomes /ʒ/: “ex-cue-zhoo”. The noun “an excuse” ends in /s/, but the exclamation uses the verb. The voiced /ʒ/ makes the phrase sound sharper, which suits its sarcastic use.
quests.phoneticRule: The verb “excuse” ends in /z/ (the noun in /s/), so the voicing of the blend depends on which word it is.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “frightened you” fits “Oh no, I frightened you”?
options: “fry-tnd-you”: both sounds are kept apart
“fry-tnd-cha”: they blend into /tʃ/
“fry-tn-ya”: the /d/ is dropped and the /j/ is kept
“fry-tnd-ja”: the final /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: “fry-tnd-ja”: the final /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/
quests.hint: Notice that “frightened” ends with a /d/ sound, then decide what a /d/ becomes before /j/.
quests.explanation: “Frightened” ends in /d/, so “frightened you” blends the /d/ and /j/ into /dʒ/: “fry-tnd-ja”. Reactions and apologies are said quickly, so recognising the blend helps you understand what the speaker did. The pattern is the same as in “did you” and “told you”.
quests.phoneticRule: Regular past-tense /d/ endings in apologies and explanations blend with “you” in the same way as other /d/ + /j/ sequences.

quests.instruction: Predict the blend in “surprise you” in “Zoe, did that surprise you?”
options: /ʒ/, because “surprise” ends in the voiced fricative /z/
/ʃ/, because “surprise” ends in a voiceless fricative
/dʒ/, because the final sound of “surprise” is a voiced stop
/tʃ/, because the final sound of “surprise” is a voiceless stop
quests.correctAnswer: /ʒ/, because “surprise” ends in the voiced fricative /z/
quests.hint: Name the last sound of “surprise” and its two features, then match them to the blend.
quests.explanation: “Surprise” ends in /z/, a voiced fricative. Voiced fricative + /j/ gives the voiced fricative /ʒ/: “sur-prai-zhoo”. The two-feature test from earlier levels works for a new word, even if you have not heard the phrase before.
quests.phoneticRule: Applying the two-feature test (manner and voicing) predicts the blend for any word ending in /t d s z/.

quests.instruction: Predict the blend in “race you” in “Race you to the car!”
options: /ʒ/, because “race” ends in a voiced fricative
/dʒ/, because “race” ends in a voiced stop
/tʃ/, because “race” ends in a voiceless stop
/ʃ/, because “race” ends in the voiceless fricative /s/
quests.correctAnswer: /ʃ/, because “race” ends in the voiceless fricative /s/
quests.hint: Use the same test: manner and voicing of the first sound.
quests.explanation: “Race” ends in /s/, a voiceless fricative. With /j/ it blends to the voiceless /ʃ/: “ray-shoo”. A playful challenge like this is said quickly, so the blend is very likely. If you had expected a /ʒ/, remember that voicing is copied, and /s/ is voiceless.
quests.phoneticRule: A voiceless fricative gives a voiceless blend (/ʃ/), and a voiced fricative gives a voiced blend (/ʒ/).

quests.instruction: Predict the blend in “thought you” in “Thought you knew that”.
options: /dʒ/, because “thought” ends in a voiced stop
/tʃ/, because “thought” ends in the voiceless stop /t/
/ʃ/, because “thought” ends in a voiceless fricative
/ʒ/, because “thought” ends in a voiced fricative
quests.correctAnswer: /tʃ/, because “thought” ends in the voiceless stop /t/
quests.hint: Apply the test to the final /t/ of “thought”: stop or fricative, voiced or voiceless?
quests.explanation: “Thought” ends in /t/, a voiceless stop. A voiceless stop + /j/ gives /tʃ/: “thaw-choo”. The spelling “ough” is irrelevant; only the final sound counts. Phrases like this are very common in everyday speech.
quests.phoneticRule: The blend is predicted from the final sound, not the spelling: words ending in /t/ give /tʃ/ even when the spelling is irregular.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “get you” fits “Let me get you a coffee”?
quests.word: Let me get you a coffee
quests.textToSpeak: Let me get you a coffee
options: “get-you”: both sounds are fully pronounced
“ge-joo”: the blend is /dʒ/
“ge-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
“ge-shoo”: the blend is /ʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “ge-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: Think of the offer as friendly and quick. Say “get you” and listen for a “ch”.
quests.explanation: “Get” ends in /t/ and “you” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /tʃ/: “ge-choo”. Offers like this are said quickly in cafés and homes, so the blend is typical. The pronoun is the trigger, and “you” is also the object of “get” here.
quests.phoneticRule: Object “you” after a verb ending in /t/ is a typical blending context: verb + you gives /tʃ/ at normal speed.

quests.instruction: In “Allow me to tell you”, why does “tell you” not blend into a new sound?
options: The /l/ is a lateral, not /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/, so the /j/ stays a glide
“tell” is a verb, and verbs cannot blend with a following pronoun
The /l/ is voiced, so it blends into /ʒ/ before “you”
The pronoun “you” is stressed after “tell”, and stress blocks every blend in English
quests.correctAnswer: The /l/ is a lateral, not /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/, so the /j/ stays a glide
quests.hint: Think about which kinds of consonant can blend with /j/, and where /l/ fits.
quests.explanation: Only /t/, /d/, /s/ and /z/ blend with /j/. The /l/ at the end of “tell” is a lateral, so “tell you” keeps a separate /j/: “tel-yoo”. Hearing a clear /j/ is therefore a clue that the first word did not end in one of the four triggers.
quests.phoneticRule: The blend rule is specific: laterals, nasals and liquids do not blend with /j/, so a clear /j/ signals a non-trigger consonant.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “hurt you” fits “Nothing will hurt you here”?
options: “hurt-you”: both sounds are separate
“hur-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
“hur-joo”: the blend is /dʒ/
“hur-shoo”: the blend is /ʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “hur-choo”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: A reassuring sentence is usually spoken softly and quickly. Predict the blend from the last sound of “hurt”.
quests.explanation: “Hurt” ends in /t/, so “hurt you” blends into /tʃ/: “hur-choo”. In British English the /r/ is silent before the consonant, so the vowel is the long /ɜː/ with no /r/. The same blend appears in “get you” and “thought you”.
quests.phoneticRule: The blend rule does not depend on the preceding vowel or on a silent /r/; only the final consonant counts.

quests.instruction: Which two blends are heard in “Nina, did you miss your bus?”
quests.word: Nina, did you miss your bus
quests.textToSpeak: Nina, did you miss your bus
options: /tʃ/ in “did you” and also /ʃ/ in “miss your”
/dʒ/ in “did you” and also /ʒ/ in “miss your”
Only “did you” blends; “miss your” keeps a clear /j/
/dʒ/ in “did you” and /ʃ/ in “miss your”
quests.correctAnswer: /dʒ/ in “did you” and /ʃ/ in “miss your”
quests.hint: Check the first sound of each blend separately.
quests.explanation: “Did” ends in the voiced stop /d/, so “did you” gives /dʒ/. “Miss” ends in the voiceless fricative /s/, so “miss your” gives /ʃ/. So the sentence is heard as “di-ja mi-shyer bus”. Two different results in one question show how the system works.
quests.phoneticRule: Each blend in a sentence follows from its own first sound, so one sentence can combine /dʒ/ and /ʃ/.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “was your” fits “Hugo, was your train late?”
options: “woz-your”: both words are strong and separate
“wo-jyer”: they blend into /dʒ/
“wo-zhyer”: the /z/ and a weak “your” blend into /ʒ/
“wo-shyer”: they blend into /ʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “wo-zhyer”: the /z/ and a weak “your” blend into /ʒ/
quests.hint: The first word ends in a voiced fricative. Predict the blend before reading the options.
quests.explanation: “Was” ends in /z/, so with weak “your” it blends into /ʒ/: “wo-zhyer”. The same applies to “is your” and “does your”. Questions about someone’s belongings, such as trains and phones, make heavy use of this pattern.
quests.phoneticRule: Auxiliary and linking verbs ending in /z/ blend with “your”, so questions about possession often contain /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: In “Zoe, did you see your boss?”, which junction does not blend?
quests.word: Zoe, did you see your boss
quests.textToSpeak: Zoe, did you see your boss
options: “see your”: “see” ends in a vowel, so only a glide appears
“did you”, because “did” is unstressed
Both blend: “did you” into /dʒ/ and “see your” into /ʒ/ as well
“did you”, because it is a question
quests.correctAnswer: “see your”: “see” ends in a vowel, so only a glide appears
quests.hint: Check whether each first word ends in one of the four triggers: /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/.
quests.explanation: “Did you” blends because “did” ends in /d/. “See your” does not, because “see” ends in a vowel; the /j/ is simply linked with a glide: “see-yer”. So one question can contain a blend and an ordinary link.
quests.phoneticRule: Words ending in vowels do not trigger coalescence; they link with a glide before /j/-initial words.

quests.instruction: Which result fits the blend in “Omar, had you met her before?”
quests.word: Omar, had you met her before
quests.textToSpeak: Omar, had you met her before
options: /tʃ/: “had” ends in a voiceless stop sound
/dʒ/: “had” ends in the voiced stop /d/
/ʃ/: “had” ends in a voiceless fricative
/ʒ/: “had” ends in a voiced fricative sound
quests.correctAnswer: /dʒ/: “had” ends in the voiced stop /d/
quests.hint: Identify the final consonant of “had”, then apply the two-feature test.
quests.explanation: “Had” ends in /d/, a voiced stop, so the blend is /dʒ/: “ha-joo”. The rest of the sentence has no /j/ trigger. Recognising the blend, then naming the first sound, is the skill this stage trains.
quests.phoneticRule: To identify a blend, name the first sound of the pair and apply the manner and voicing rule.

quests.instruction: Compare “hit you” in “Kate, who hit you?” with “hid you”. How do the two blends differ?
options: They give the same blend, because the vowel in both words is the same short vowel /ɪ/
“hit you” gives /dʒ/ and “hid you” gives /tʃ/, the other way round
Neither blends, because both words are short and strongly stressed
“hit you” gives voiceless /tʃ/ and “hid you” gives voiced /dʒ/; only voicing differs
quests.correctAnswer: “hit you” gives voiceless /tʃ/ and “hid you” gives voiced /dʒ/; only voicing differs
quests.hint: Compare the last sounds of “hit” and “hid”. What single feature differs?
quests.explanation: “Hit” ends in voiceless /t/ and “hid” in voiced /d/. The blend copies that voicing: /tʃ/ for “hit you” and /dʒ/ for “hid you”. The vowel does not affect it. This is the same voicing rule you used for /s/ and /z/.
quests.phoneticRule: A minimal pair differing only in voicing at the end of the first word produces blends that differ only in voicing.

quests.instruction: Which results fit “miss your” and “won’t you” in “Priya, you’ll miss your flight, won’t you?”
quests.word: Priya, you’ll miss your flight, won’t you
quests.textToSpeak: Priya, you’ll miss your flight, won’t you
options: /tʃ/ in “miss your” and /ʃ/ in “won’t you”
/ʃ/ in “miss your” and /dʒ/ in “won’t you”
/ʃ/ in “miss your” and /tʃ/ in “won’t you”
/ʒ/ in “miss your” and /tʃ/ in “won’t you”
quests.correctAnswer: /ʃ/ in “miss your” and /tʃ/ in “won’t you”
quests.hint: Take each junction in turn: name the final sound of “miss” and of “won’t”.
quests.explanation: “Miss” ends in voiceless /s/, giving /ʃ/. “Won’t” ends in voiceless /t/, giving /tʃ/. Both blends are voiceless because both first sounds are voiceless. This stage-check sentence combines two different results from one rule.
quests.phoneticRule: Two voiceless triggers in one sentence give two voiceless blends, /ʃ/ and /tʃ/, according to their manner.
